Since the staff is mentioned twice in a single sentence, would you tell us which staff did you have in mind? And I'll read out the sentence in English so that you can get a correct interpretation. [In English] "What it says in the decision probably reflect the fact that when it was impossible for the staff to meet, the staff decided to relieve me the duties of commander of Territorial Defence. And I received this decision precisely on this date, the 29th of May." [Interpretation] So will you tell us which staff could no longer meet?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that it couldn't, but perhaps a meeting of the Crisis Staff had taken place meanwhile, and the decision was taken already on the 12th and later on about the abolition of the Territorial Defence and all these resubordinations and I received the decision on 15th, and I thought it was late because I received it on the 29th. I thought it was simply the administration which was late, but then I realised that the decisions were being taken at the time. And I said I thought that it was a long period of time, between the 12th and the 15th of May, I mean the order of the commander, and so it would have been logical for me to have received it then. So that is how I interpreted it. But I perhaps got the dates wrong. My apologies to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that your staff, either the staff of the Territorial Defence after the 17th of May, 1992, could not meet since it no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't meet much before that because there were only a few people there who issued certificates and drivers who took food and so on. But right. Well, it existed officially as a staff. And after that, it had no further role because simply became a logistics base which took care of distribution of food and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 20 of yesterday's transcript, line 25, His Honour Judge Schomburg asks you whether every crime should have been reported to the police or investigating bodies in person or by telephone. And I'm asking you if it is everybody's duty, every citizen's duty, be he a plain civilian or a member of the Crisis Staff, to report a crime? And your answer was yes. And that is - I'm sorry I'm testifying, but - in line with positive regulations of the former Yugoslavia and the present Bosnia-Herzegovina. I will ask you, is it necessary to report facts that are common knowledge? And I'll give you an example. For instance, there is a flood in the town of Prijedor. Is it your duty to take a boat to go to the police and report to them about the flood?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right. For such a serious man, this question is not serious, but you must have some reason for it. Sorry that I'm talking like this; I'm not criticising you really. But there is a service that take cares of that, and they measure the level of water and so on and so forth. This is not something that happens in 10 minutes' time. It happens over a day or a night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. That the -- that is the direction that I wanted to go in. Does one have to inform the police about crimes committed by the police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, that is another curious question, I think. But the police know what they do, I suppose there would inform each other mutually or rather report to each other. Brief, they make some sort of official record and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware whether in the spring and summer of 1992, there were attempts to conceal crimes by the police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly yes. I can't really say anything specific. I can't remember such instances, but it happened perhaps. I can't affirm that, but.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the military report about their activities to civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the combat operations and if you mean Prijedor, I don't think that the military submitted reports or inform about their military, about their military business, the civilian authorities. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, is it also true that the civilians were not even allowed to be in the theatres of operations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat operations, wartime operations were far away from Prijedor, and the civilians didn't go there. And at the time when there was fighting there, civilians were on one side, and the military were on the other. Whether there was some mixing, I cannot really say, but I know the civilians were here, and the military were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crime on Mount Vlasic, or to be more accurate, at Koricanske Stijene happened around the 21st of August, 1992. You were asked if you knew whether this was discussed by the Crisis Staff, and I will ask you whether you know that the Crisis Staff stopped its operation on the 27th of July, 1992 when its decisions, taken between the 29th of May and the 24th of July, 1992, were forwarded to the -- were submitted to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor for adoption? Are you aware that the Crisis Staff stopped its work on the 27th of July? If you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I do know is that the war presidency came into being, but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'd like to ask the usher to show you Exhibit S68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the meantime I take the opportunity to ask you the following question: Wasn't it true, Mr. Kuruzovic, that under the rules and the manual for Yugoslavia, any person serving in the army had the obligation to report any kind of crimes committed in the army to the responsible authorities, especially the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know those military laws. But it stands to logic that there was such a decision. And in the army, there were also -- there were also services responsible for security matters. That is what they are called. They are controlling the work of all sorts of things, so it is quite possible, but I am not really familiar with those regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, on page 23 of yesterday's transcript, line 13, His Honour Judge Schomburg asks you: "How is it possible that the president of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic, should order, and then comes the quote "it is ordered the military police and the agencies of the public security station Prijedor are ordered" as we can see 91 of this document..." To begin with, in relation to the question of His Honour Judge Schomburg whether Dr. Stakic in the Crisis Staff -- took decisions alone in the Crisis Staff or whether the Crisis Staff took decisions as a body?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a body, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we talked yesterday about the type of document that this document is, I'd like to ask you, what is it the unity of command in the army and the police and does this unity of command allow anyone to interfere into the issue of orders outside of the chains of command in the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not think so, except unless we are dealing with some Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 14692 to 14707. civilian matters, seized property or something. So somebody has to ask that his property be protected, and the police have to do it. And if it is not done, then somebody has to ask or request or order that it be done. But it has nothing to do with the safety of people or anything, especially if this was done by members of the police or army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us assume that this order was -- not this particular order, that it was not executed. Would a member of the police for failing to comply with this order be charged by the military prosecutor and brought before the military court? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. I do not -- I think that he might be charged, and then tried if he failed to comply with the military order. But not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, we won't be needing this document any more. But could the usher please now show the witness Document S70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of the 6th of June, 1992 which specifies that the blockade of the town remains in force. And you explained to us who was the one who had the -- who controlled -- who carried out the control at the checkpoints, that it was done under the regional command together with the police.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the army had to issue an order to its units and the police likewise had to issue an order to its units which factually carried out that control?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I didn't see those orders, but I'm sure that such orders arrived, seeing that there is this conclusion. That is, those who are doing this are requested to do that. And at some point, it stops because the army cannot block the town until cows come home or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the Crisis Staff in this way address the citizenry, the civilian population of Prijedor, and did it also address the citizenry with proclamations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I suppose so. I can't remember it any longer, because it was a long time ago. But it was to the either Kozarski Vjesnik, because it never stopped coming out, or the radio. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't be needing this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I believe it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Lukic, how long you will need for the completion of your line of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope less than an hour. Maybe not more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Only that the Prosecution is prepared to start their line of questions already this afternoon. We'll start after the break immediately in closed session, and only five minutes later, we'll ask the witness to enter the courtroom. The trial stays adjourned until 2.00 sharp. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Kuruzovic, may I ask, are you prepared to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like the usher to show the witness the Exhibit Number S69.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kuruzovic, this document was also discussed, and the Honourable Chamber put some questions to you about this document. This is an order on supplies for the troops of the army and the police with oil. Is it correct that at that time, there was a shortage of oil and oil derivatives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that neither a natural or a legal person was in a position to obtain ample quantities of oil or sufficient quantities of oil for that matter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In such conditions which are worse than usual conditions, was it necessary to order anybody to get oil? In other words, is it correct that everybody wanted to have more oil and oil derivatives than could be provided to them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody wanted more than they could have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will be moving on to another topic. I have some questions regarding the functioning of the Municipal Assembly. On page 45, line 25, the Honourable Judge Vassylenko asked you: "Is it correct that the main political decisions on most important things were made by the leadership of the SDS, and that these decisions were later on implemented by the civilian authorities, by the police and the army?" Were you a member of the SDS leadership at any level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then correct that you wouldn't know what decisions were made by the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can just assume. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the majority of professional officers in the spring and summer of 1992 were actually members of the League of Communists movement for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that decisions in the army were made aside from the decisions made by the SDS, or at least they were not coming their way from the SDS? You can also say that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it was not the party that was in a position to issue any orders to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 46, a monoparty system is mentioned in line 6. Are you aware of the fact that some members of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor were not members of the SDS? For example, Slavko Budimir, Ranko Travar, Vojo Pavicic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Pavicic and Travar, I can accept that, although I personally don't know. For Slavko Budimir, I don't know. No, I don't know about the first two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, managers of the largest companies such as the iron ore mine Ljubija, there was Mr. Ostoja Marjanovic who was not a member of the SDS. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are just some of the names that I managed to collect during the break. So can we then conclude that it was possible to have people as officials in the municipality and people in the managerial positions of various companies who were not members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, His Honour Judge Vassylenko on page 49, line 25, asked you whether it was true that the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor had become the only official body of Prijedor Municipality. Were the bodies such as the secretariat for people's defence, the police, the army, the courts, the prosecutor's office, the Executive Board were they also official bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I said what I meant, and that is that the majority of the Executive Board members were also members of the Crisis Staff. The only thing that I was confused about were the dates when things happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you something about the open centre Trnopolje. When you arrived in the open centre Trnopolje on the request of Simo Drljaca and Mico Kovacevic as you have explained to us, were there already people there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found a group of women, children, and elderly there. They had arrived by lorries and tractors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you went there together with ten more people from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There were maybe two or three of us. Actually, I don't remember who was with me. I took my car and went there to check whether things were as they were represented to me. When I saw how things were, I don't know whether I sent for somebody or maybe the following morning, we brought some ten people who would provide security for the people. Or maybe people arrived during that night. I can't remember. At that time, when I arrived, with me was one of my colleagues from school, Mr. Rifat Kurtovic who was helping me with these vehicles and people who were accommodated in the neighbouring houses, and there was no need at the time to take anybody to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that only for the first few days, the security was provided by people from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After a few days, the security was provided by the 43rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know when this happened, whether it was after two or three days, but very quickly after that, there were already a number of people. The security had to be stepped up. I've already said that one of the members of the police from the local police unit was shot from a wagon that was standing in the railway station. I realised then that things would get serious and that I had to step up security and that I had to provide more guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the policeman Banovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember his name. I know that he was a Serbian member of the police who was killed. I don't know whether it was on the following day or when it was. I know it was during the daytime, but I can't remember exactly when that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked for the Red Cross to arrive in Trnopolje immediately.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the men who arrived with me was a member of the Red Cross anyway. But on the following day, the president or the secretary of the Red Cross, Mladen Zoric arrived, and a few more volunteers. There were four or five women among them and some doctors, so people were received by them. On the following day or one day after that, or maybe on the same day, a doctor came from Kozarac with a nurse, one nurse or two nurses, and a male nurse. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the very beginning, did the Red Cross bring food and baby food?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, at the very beginning, they brought food and powdered milk. There was a surgery over there that worked normally and the doctors opened their office in that surgery, and they started seeing people and administering medical care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When people -- when did the people from the Red Cross of Banja Luka arrive?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I don't know the exact date, but very soon after the establishment of this open centre. At that time, it was not an open centre, it was just a place where people took refuge. And a few days after we opened the centre, the representatives of the UNHCR and the Red Cross came together. And from then on, they would visit the centre every morning. And they provided a lot of assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people from the International Red Cross also bring a table which read in both English and Serbian "the open centre Trnopolje"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that they would come together in the morning, and some people who were from the UNHCR had interpreters with them, and there were also one or two people from the Red Cross. And they brought this table together. Now, who it was who wrote that inscription on the table, I don't know. I believe that it was the Red Cross. It was written in two languages. It was a white table with blue -- with the blue inscription, blue letters that we put up in one place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the representatives of these international organisations immediately explain to you that according to the Geneva Convention, you were under the obligation to make a list of people in that centre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the very first day, they told us that. And immediately, they asked us to do that. And they asked us to urgently bring certificates that these people were there. And they provided us with certificates which were, I believe, in our own language, and we -- they made a lot of copies of all sorts of certificates, and these were filled in there. And then the whole families would fill out these forms so that it was well known who was there. And they explained to us that it was according to the Geneva Conventions, and they asked me to sign my name as the person who was providing for the security of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People from the local Red Cross, did they immediately proceed to take record of the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning, where did people who were accommodated there get the food from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first day, the food was provided by the Red Cross in the morning already. But I returned, and when during the day more people came, a hundred or more, I don't know, I immediately went to the Executive Board and requested their assistance that they ask bread from Zitopromet. It's a bakery. And I think that Ranko Travar was the man who was in charge of those things. He had ordered that from the mine canteen, food be brought so that cooked food was brought from the mine canteen there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the number of people increased, were some kitchens organised there in the yard?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I requested from the brigade commander to turn over two army kitchens where it is easy to make fire and prepare large quantities of food. And people volunteered. There wasn't enough meat there. And one man there, I can't remember what his name was, I think his name was Hilmija, Hilmija Lokic from Suvi Brod, he volunteered to slaughter a cow or an ox at his home in order to provide -- to supply meat. And people were ordered to go home and bring in livestock which had remained alone there and nobody was feeding that livestock there at home, to bring them there so that we had some milk. And every day, one of the heads of this cattle was slaughtered, and that is how people were fed. And the other vitamins, that is the green vegetables and all that, they picked that in the neighbourhood, later on, they went home, they'd take a wheelbarrow, go get it, bring it and cook it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a shortage of water or was it -- was the water supply satisfactory and how was that done?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was water. All the houses had water. Most of them had outdoor pumps, so that those could be used. And there was also water in the school. I mean, it was switched on to the water mains. But it was hot. It was summer. So that people needed to wash themselves more often for reasons of hygiene. And therefore, we asked representatives of the International Red Cross, if they could, to bring over a water tanker or something so that more water would be there and to take more water from those pumps so that people wouldn't have to stay at those pumps all the time. And they were happy to do that. And immediately I think brought a 2 tonne or 1 tonne plastic cisterns which were filled up and they put them on a balcony, and they also brought hoses. And this is a curious fact. There are faucets, about ten of them could be screwed on, and one could draw water from ten faucets at a time, and people then had plastic canisters, something, and that is how they took water. That is that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who filled this water container?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A water tanker came from Prijedor, from the fire brigade, with water which comes from the town water supply. And that water was used. And I forgot to say, the very next day, well, perhaps it wasn't the next day, but it was on the third or the fourth day because it was very hot, before those water containers arrived, nevertheless, those water tankers arrived in case of a shortage. And later on, it also continued to come because it was very hot and people had to wash themselves and do the dishes and such like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people who were in the centre, non-Serbs, could they go out to fetch water or collect food?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not in a prison. They could go wherever they liked. And especially of evening, it was interesting to see because people walked around and sang and made their national dishes, fluff pastry and what else. They made their coffee. They could leave the school or those buildings they were in and would go towards their homes where they used to live before or to visit their neighbours or friends further away from the centre. And they would get vegetables from there and bring them back to use for food. And nobody else could get there because the army was guarding them there, so they didn't stay at home, in their proper homes. And of course, the International Red Cross, it was important to know that the International Red Cross and the UNHCR came there every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after they would collect food and the necessary -- and the requisite water, did they come back on their own?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nobody escorted them, so they would go on their own and come back on their own. In the beginning, they did not venture further afield, not further than 100, 200 metres. But since the number of people increased, of course, one needed to procure food that was of high quality. Potatoes and carrots and cabbage and parsley and whatnot. So they went three or four kilometres out into the field with a wheelbarrow to get that food, and they would get it and come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the attack on Prijedor, did the number of people increase?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, but perhaps a day or two later, during the attack itself, as far as I know, the army had ordered, they went to look for those who had perpetrated the attack around Stari Grad because it is across the Sana. And part of the populace from there came. Some came by train. And later on, as those had fled across the Sana towards Hambarine, and then the army went out to mop up the ground, and I believe there were about 2 or 3 busloads of people. They came with their families, with their children, and that is how they got away safely from combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to people to tell them not to come to the centre any more because there was no room for more?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases when they would come right there to the centre, and I wasn't very happy to see them come there, but I had no say in that because those from the Red Cross were deciding about it even. And we were quite clear that there were already enough people, that the weather was hot. And a few days later, we didn't have any requests from people to leave. But some seven or eight days later, people already started coming to ask to go to Zenica, or rather to the areas of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina with the majority Muslim population. And I think that on two occasions, they thus left by train to Zenica and then those would not allow to enter, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who is Mr. Mignon and whether he spoke to people in the centre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so. I thought his name was Migon, but obviously I mispronounced him. Perhaps he was a Mignon. I think he was the head of the International Red Cross office in Banja Luka, and those visits became -- those requests to leave were too frequent because very many of them were not interested in going to Central Bosnia, they wanted to go abroad. And at our -- and then we asked him and the Red Cross asked him to come, and he went to Trnopolje and spoke with those people. And at some point he got angry and he said: "Well, you have come here on your own, most of you on your own volition, and now you are asking me that I ship you all over Europe. We can't do it. We are here to help you as much as we can." I can't remember him really verbatim, but it was something along those lines that he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there perhaps instances when people who were in the centre in Trnopolje had visits from the relatives in Prijedor who brought them food?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't instances. It happened on a daily basis. The train would come from Prijedor, and this is the Kozarac station some hundred metres fifty away from school. Perhaps 200 metres away. So that people came from the town, those who had stayed in their homes and flats because some had left their homes and flats. I don't know whether there were some family understandings. Some people would come over here and some people would stay there. And so perhaps when it became possible for them to leave, they would get together and leave. But they brought lots of food and fruit, and as I've already said, those ethnic dishes, and they often invited us to join them and those from the Red Cross, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move freely among those people without any personal -- without any bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day, I'd go often to the cultural centre, or perhaps to the cooperative, and I frequently did that, and especially to the school, just to make sure that there were no problems with the hygiene or anything because after all there were many people and although the school was built as it was built nevertheless there were many people and I always went there alone. And nobody even said an ugly word to me, let alone attacked me, so that I never had any clash, any argument with them or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And people who brought food for the relatives in the centre, were they free? Could they go back home?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were free to return home, but there were also those who came on bicycles, and I've already told you there was a group of people from Petrov Gaj, and perhaps Gornji Garevci or I don't know which place exactly. But they often came on bicycles to bring food and then I had to ask the commanders of the security to send a few soldiers there. And once I requested the commander of the military police, and they found that man and found several bicycles there. And they detained him and took him to Prijedor. How he ended up later, I don't know how long he spent in prison but I know he was in prison because of that. And that was one such man. Now, what was his name? Something beginning with c, Cavic or something, yes. Later on I heard that he also committed a murder, I think. After when the centre had ceased to exist, he killed, I think, one or two official policemen because the neighbourhood community centre was there and a couple of people worked there or perhaps they even had their families there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people from the UNHCR present there every time a convoy left Trnopolje regardless of whether it had been organised by them or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if they were there every time, but they were there very often, both they and the Red Cross, and the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the testimony of another witness, an etymological moot point emerged in the interpretation from our language into English. Does -- is there any similarity in our language between the term "reception centre" and the reception desk in a hotel, say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, of course they are different. They have nothing in common whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you because when it is translated into English, it almost sounds identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kuruzovic, thank you. For the time being, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Kuruzovic, now we'll follow the line of questions put to you by the Prosecution, as it's already now the third day of your testimony, I want to recall all the informations I gave you in the beginning, especially that it's your right, if you so want, to remain silent, also to remain silent in those cases where you believe that a question -- that an answer to a question would tend to self-incriminate you. And if there should be any problem, don't hesitate to contact us. If you need any assistance, you will get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, please. Questioned by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, towards the end of his examination today, Mr. Lukic asked you whether you had any bodyguards in the Trnopolje camp. You answered that no one attacked or insulted you among the Muslims. But you did not answer his question. Did you have any bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I mean yes, I understood what he asked me. I had two men who were with me there often. But when I moved among the people there in the school, in the cultural centre, I had no need for any guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your bodyguards were the twin brothers Balaban. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at what period of time were you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly. I think as of spring 1991, perhaps March is when I became a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remain a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you were in Croatia. At that time, were you in -- can you explain what you were doing. Were you part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I mentioned that. I don't know which period of time do you have in mind. Oh, you mean when I took those people along so that they could see how those houses in that village were destroyed. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me go back before that. Were you a member of the JNA? In the 1990s, were you ever a member of the JNA since 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until -- until 15th or the 16th when the order was issued for me to join the regional command, until then, I was a member of the Territorial Defence. And before that, five or six years before that, I was part of the JNA officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the Territorial Defence, or as a member of any other military or paramilitary unit, did you take part in fighting in Croatia, or were you at the front in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, with the 343rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, the brigade was part of the 5th Krajina Corps as it was called at that time commanded by various people including at the end General Talic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Lukic asked you about political parties having influence on the army. Can you tell me, in 1991 as a member of the JNA, what political body controlled or what institution, civilian institution, controlled the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, Bosnia and Herzegovina, because that is the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not exist. That is, the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, just for an example, I'm now talking about 1991 when the JNA fought Croatian forces in the Krajina -- the Croatian Krajina, Serb Krajina in Croatia. At that time, the president of Yugoslavia was de facto the commander in chief of the JNA. Correct? Excuse me, he was de jure, he was according to the law, the commander in chief of the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I presume so. I don't really know the constitution of the former Yugoslavia by heart, but I think that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, the president of Yugoslavia at the time the conflict broke out was Stipe Mesic, a representative of Croatian ethnicity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, wasn't it obvious to everyone in 1991 and 1992 that the JNA and later the VRS was taking the sides of certain nationalist parties and was not controlled by the president of Yugoslavia, in the case of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a major political issue. I cannot answer those questions in the way that you'd like to hear me answer them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in Prijedor, let's go down to Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only one correction, although the witness has already answered, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, no correction. Only objections are allowed. You are not testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question put by my learned friend is not based on facts. Mr. Mesic was not president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: President of the presidency. I'll enter a stipulation that he was president of the presidency of the federal Yugoslavia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in Prijedor, was there close cooperation between the SDS and the 343rd, later the 43rd, Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. I don't know about the official bodies. I was not a member of any leading bodies. I was not a leader of the Serbian Democratic Party. So what the real relationship between the SDS and the brigade was, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. We'll come back to that in a moment. First I want to step back. You were asked a few questions about the census in Prijedor. And recognising you're not an expert, I'm not asking for your opinion about the results, but I want to ask you what was the popular perception among Serbs about the results? Were they upset, the Serbian population, and particularly other members of the SDS, with the results of the census showing for the first time that Muslims had a plurality in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that one could say that they were upset, but I also don't believe that they believed the figures and that they believed there was such a prevalence of Muslims over the Serbs. And there were talks around the town that something was wrong with that census and that the figures had been tampered with. I did not have any possibility to check any of those figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt once again. Maybe it was mispronounced by you, Mr. Koumjian. On page 71, line 25, it reads "plurality." Didn't you want to say "majority"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, I believe I meant plurality. They had the highest percentage but less than 50 per cent, as I recall, of the population. Plurality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the relative majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, going to the 1990 elections, is it correct - there's evidence in this case - that the SDA party won a majority -- excuse me, again, a plurality of the seats in the assembly, they won 30 seats, the SDS, 28; the HDZ, 2; and the other parties, mainly leftist parties, 30 seats, in Prijedor. A few questions about those results. First, sir, given the results nationwide or public wide in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it be correct that the left bloc, the nonnationalists won many more seats in Prijedor than they did in the rest of the republic where in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina they only held about 10 per cent of the seats after the election?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm listening to you, but I don't know what you're asking me. I am not aware of these figures. I don't know them off my head. But I know that the Muslim population had the relative majority, and the others had fewer seats. And I agree with you that this is what the situation was and that this was the balance of political forces in the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it also correct, as I stated, that the nonnationalist parties had a much stronger showing in Prijedor, where they won one-third of the seats, than they did republicwide where they won only about 10 per cent of the seats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't like you using the word "nationalist parties." Maybe you could say national parties because all of these parties, the SDS, SDA, and HDZ, were national parties. And probably meant the national parties, the SDS and HDZ, got fewer votes, and you're right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll definitely adopt your terminology. Thank you for that correction. Sir, following these results, apparently at some time, there was a decision to form a Serbian government separate from the government that was elected by the multiethnic assembly, on the 7th of January, 1991. Is it correct, sir, that even before that time, members of the SDS were making preparations for conflict, armed conflict, with the other ethnic groups in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a very difficult question. I have told you that people were arming themselves in huge numbers, Croats, and especially Muslims did that. And faced with such a situation, I know that the Serbs also armed themselves. But there is also the fact that they all had arms from the Territorial Defence, across the board. But as far as I could understand you, you're talking about the entire state, and you allege that the Serbs were getting ready for an armed conflict. I don't know what you can base this statement on. I don't know why you can say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try for the rest of my questions to confine myself to Prijedor, and that question was confined to Prijedor. Unless I say otherwise, I mean only Prijedor. And I'll try to be even more specific. Sir, isn't it true that Simo Drljaca was forming a separate Serb police as early as the fall of 1991 in preparation for conflict with the other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honest to God, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified on your -- well, in your radio interview that was played during the first day of your testimony, you talked about the Serbs being organised in every village, on S91. What did you mean when you said that the Serbs were organised in every village?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how things are. When there are wolves, people get organised to protect their families from wolves. I've told you that when people learned that in the suburbs of the town and in the neighbouring villages, in those enclaves, either through the SDA, the Muslims and Croats were arming themselves, then the Serbs also did the same, to protect their families. But as far as I know, there were no activities involving fire weapons. I took the oath here to tell the truth, and I can say under the solemn declaration that nobody used firearms against anybody, either the Serbs against the Muslims or vice versa. Such things did not happen in our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like the usher to hand out a newspaper article from Kozarski Vjesnik entitled: "Memories on April's events in 1992." And I believe it's dated the 28th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's being handed out, sir, who was Dusan Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Jankovic, I don't know exactly, but I believe that he was the commander of a police station in the Security Services Centre. I believe that they are -- they have different duties. Some are in charge of traffic. Some are in charge of general crimes. But I believe that he was the commander of a public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... S430A and B respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, Miroslav Paras is a name familiar to you. He was a police officer that you saw at the Trnopolje camp when you were there, correct? And excuse me, just so that there's no arguments, I will call it the Trnopolje centre. At the Trnopolje centre, sir, you saw Mr. Paras, Miroslav Paras. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? [Realtime transcript read in error "Yes"]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a commander of the intervention squad or one of its members. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible. I don't know the structure, and I don't know who the commander was because I had nothing whatsoever to do with the police, except when I asked for escorts for those people who were leaving towards Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's intervention, the answer appears as "yes," and the answer by the witness was "where". That is 22., 15:25:56.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear for the record, because there appears to be an error in the transcript, when I asked you whether you saw Miroslav Paras the policeman at the Trnopolje centre, what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what he looks like. I may have seen him, but I don't remember him. I'm sorry. Give me a minute to try and remember. I believe that he was one of the policemen who got killed, a fair-haired one. They are much younger people than me. I do have a vague recollection of his face, and the name does ring a very distant bell, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, at the time that this article was published in Kozarski Vjesnik, did you have a position with that newspaper in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was the director of that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the article entitled "memories on April's events in 1992," I'd like to read out, and you can read along with me, the first two sentences under the paragraph that appears in bold "establishment of SJB Prijedor." "The idea to form a Serb public security station that will work and act illegally appeared in the beginning of November and had been realised on 10 November, 1991. Checked group of men led by Dusan Jankovic formed 11 illegal war police stations soon. Right in the beginning, the hardest tasks were performed successfully. Cooperation with the army was great, what accomplished better work of Prijedor's police." As translated. Sir, do you have any comment upon -- were you aware that Mr. Jankovic formed 11 illegal Serb police stations beginning in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honest to God, I didn't know that. I don't know why this would be necessary. I believe that he was a member of the police at the time in the public security centre in Prijedor. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1995 when you were the director of Kozarski Vjesnik, was it your habit to read the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. Sometimes I did, but sometimes I did not. If you had in mind this particular paper, it was the editor in chief who was supposed to read this paper. They had a meeting in the morning, an editorial meeting, and they would discuss the contents of the paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, talking a bit more about the takeover, you talked about a telegram that had been intercepted and that a decision was made to do the takeover on the night, that was in the early morning of the 30th of April, 1992, so between the 29th and 30th. Isn't it correct, Mr. Kuruzovic, that actually earlier you had planned to do the takeover on the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the discussions about the date, but I remember that we were talking about a situation, that there was anarchy, and that that situation called for the takeover of power. And this was the talk in the entire town among all the citizens because the situation was really bad. In addition to that, war raged all over the place already, and it may sound bad for me to say that, but the Serbs grazed grass in the stadium of Sarajevo and Prijedor was full of refugees from western Slavonia, from Krajina, from Central Bosnia, from Travnik, from Zenica, Bugojno, Visoko, from the western part of Bosnia, from Bihac, Cazin, and Kljuc. And people had members of family already killed, and the overall situation instilled fear among the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, going to the section of the article entitled "takeover of the authorities," that would be the fourth bolded section, I'm going to read the first paragraph of that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and read both paragraphs. That would be helpful, that we need not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Seriousness of the situation improved fast, so the realisation of takeover the authorities had been agreed for the night between 30 April and 1 May. However, on 29 April, at 1400 hours, a letter arrived in Prijedor by which Delimustafic and Jerko Doko explicitly ordered blockade of the barracks, military convoys, and transports. Due to that reason, date for takeover by the authorities was moved 24 hours, on 29/30 April, at 4.00 a.m." I have to apologise, Your Honour. Apparently this is a rough translation. I will try to get a better translation as soon as possible. "The public security station was taken as the first one in which a group of the policemen led by deceased Miroslav Paras entered without a fired bullet and by the same way all more important structure in town have been taken. A code message "taxi bar works" meant that the action of taking over the authorities in Prijedor was performed without any mistake. The day after, the Serb tricolour flag fluttered at the masts in front of the municipal building and the SJB. Congratulations from the CSB, and many SJBs of the Republic of Srpska arrived for well-done conducted task. In this way, Prijedor has become a Serb town." And sir, I'm going to ask you to read, because of the poor quality of this translation, if you look at the next section entitled "fiery action was imposed by political circumstances," could you read that section out loud beginning with Simo Drljaca's quote, then Dusan Jankovic, then Milutin Cadzo.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't seem to find it. It says here: "The MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina calls for the disarmament of Serbs," but I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it maybe here where it says the takeover of power?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the section just after what I just read. The title is something like "fiery action was imposed by political circumstances" and it begins with a quote from Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I understand now. Do you want me to read what Simo Drljaca said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The action to take over power was done impeccably, and this is corroborated by the fact that only 460 policemen participated in the execution of this operation. The operation was successful without any casualties. Together with my colleagues, Dusan Jankovic and Milutin Cadzo, I started to organise the public security centre in Prijedor. At that time, we had already had 11 Serbian police stations, and after the takeover, the stations in Kozarac and Ljubija were also established."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now if you could read Mr. Jankovic's remarks.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jankovic, you're saying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, if you could read the next two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that what it says here is that "the activity of the army during the April events had been coordinated in advance with the activities of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian police. As the first chief of the Serbian war police stations, I had been informed about my men, about everything. Already during the first meetings held in late 1991, we embarked on a decisive implementation of all the planned tasks because we were aware that there was no going back. There could not be going back. After all, every people was given to make their own decisions and choose their own way. But when it came to the Serbian staff, there could be no hesitation." Do you also want me to read what Milutin Cadzo said in the next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps in the interests of time, I'd like you to move on, please. There then is a section that appears to be an interview with you. And then the third bolded section entitled "MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina asks for disarmament of Serbs." If you could read that section, that entire section to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Before that, another interpreter's intervention if we may, the title of this passage is not "Fiery action," but a "blitz action" or a "lightning action".

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find this. Oh, I see. The attack on "BH MUP calls for the disarmament of Serbs". Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could read from that section there to the end of the article.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At one of the meetings in late April where representatives of the Serb police, the army, and the Territorial Defence were present, as well as the representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, the principle dilemma was as to when would be the most appropriate moment to carry out the takeover of power in Prijedor Municipality. The organisers of the Serb resistance were in two minds, whether to start -- embark on that action on the last day of holiday or on the first working day in the month of May. Slobodan Kuruzovic had to say this about that. So this text is the journalist's opinion and introduction of what I allegedly said: "All our fears and dilemmas were resolved by the former minister of the interior, Jerko Doko by his fax message dated 29 April, 1992, in which, amongst other things, there is an order to disarm Serb policemen, from the active and reserve forces. That should have been done by taking the SUP building and it was also envisaged that the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks would be taken. Although Jerko Doko could not even dream that this would happen, the fax was received not only by the Muslim authority in Prijedor, but also by us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could continue reading, and at the end, I'll ask you for your comments or any -- if you want to indicate whether or not you believe you said this or not. But please, continue to read.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well, then, we immediately went to Lieutenant-Colonel Vladimir Arsic, to the barracks, to ask for his advice as to what we should do. We had an opportunity to take over the power by force, but we needed a certain time to charge certain groups of people and men with certain tasks. Despite our indecisiveness, Commander Arsic managed to persuade us not to wait because that job was best done immediately. On that same night, he reminded me of many actions that had to be organised in a haste in Lipik, and successes were achieved in that way. Because in such situation, decisiveness, speed, and surprise were crucial. And that is exactly what happened. All the preparations were carried out on the same evening. We were divided into two groups, the police group and the military group. The police group was organised by Drljaca, Cadzo, and Jankovic, and the military group was organised by Captains Bojic ^, Savic ^, Karlica, Agent Nadja ^ and also by Major Rajlic and myself. This was a statement," and again these are journalist's words. "It was a statement by Slobodan Kuruzovic, the former commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence regarding some less-known detail on the organisation and takeover of power in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this article as you can see appeared in Kozarski Vjesnik of which you were the director in 1995. Is there anything in the article that you dispute?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I haven't read the whole article, I just read this part. But no, I'm not disputing any of this. As it says, when His Honour the Presiding Judge asked me, and later, and the Defence, too, they asked me the day the dispatch arrived, we read it this morning, which was ordering the disarmament of the barracks and the order to launch combat operations, and I can't remember exactly the contents of that whole order. But I saw it now in point of fact it was an order to destroy both the barracks and the troops and to take SUP. So as our people say, that was just one drop too many, and at the meeting which I attended, as you know, it was agreed that power should be taken over that night. And the police organised that. And as regards the military part, people were -- people in villages around the town were simply informed that the power would be taken over that night. And in case something happened, that they would be let know about it to take care and to guard people there, to look after the people, to avoid any casualties. But otherwise, there was no military action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, sir, I recognise this is a long article, and in fairness to you, I would ask -- tell you that we will give you an extra copy to keep with you over the weekend and to read. And on Monday, you can tell us if there are any other matters that you dispute. If there are any matters you dispute in the article. Is it correct, sir, as stated in the article that the decision about the takeover, the timing of it, was moved up 24 hours and had originally been planned for the next day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't say "planned." There was discussion about it. There was no major decision because, of course, the fear was involved. After all, it's not easy to take it over. There is the state. There is the police, this is the army. But when this dispatch arrived, it was really just too much. Concerning the attitude that this power had towards the army or the police, and they do not exist in a vacuum. There are also citizens there, people who live there. So they read that the barracks should be attacked, that everybody should be disarmed, both the military and the police, can you imagine how the Serb people received this news, I mean, the representatives of that people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, the telegram you're talking about is the one that Milos Jankovic brought to someone's attention. Is that correct? Do you know where it came from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the Ministry of Defence, from Sarajevo, and the commander of the Territorial Defence in Sarajevo. But it arrived officially because in the municipal hall, there is an official telephone. I think it's 985. And that is used for some extraordinary news, and then it is -- and then such texts are only given to the institutions indicated. So I don't know, or rather I can guess. Since Mr. Stakic was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, he was also one of those who received this dispatch, not only the president or the chief of police. And that is how the meeting was called, and people attended this meeting. Now I see that it is made of two parts, and it is much more serious. I was told about that in haste, because Simo Miskovic and I were amongst the last to arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you learned about the telegram on the 29th of April was just what you were told by Mr. Stakic. You didn't actually see the telegram yourself on the 29th. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't see it personally. I didn't hear it from him only, but also from those other present who had arrived there before me. And that meeting was a very short one. People were commenting on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the takeover, though, had been planned before the telegram arrived, correct? It's clear from this article that the takeover had been planned for the 30th, and was moved up because of the telegram. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is, and it isn't. I said that yes, it was discussed. People said it was necessary, and people were suggesting to do it during the holiday when the offices are empty, when people are not there, when to avoid any silly thing from happening. There wasn't an agreement to do it. And then two or three days before the holiday, when it arrived, then I said that, and others also think that all the dilemmas are resolved as said. That is, Jerko Doko with his cable forced us to do it, whether we liked it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 29th of April, if you could just describe for us a little bit about the conditions of the town of Prijedor. At that time - please just answer my questions briefly right now, if you can - at that time, was there water and electricity in Prijedor, on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 29th of April, at that time, why was it necessary in the view of you and the others planning a takeover to remove the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, well, water and electricity are not the only things determining living conditions. There was a notion of problems in the town which were not being solved properly. For the town to live and work, one needed to have shops open, to ensure the exchange of goods between people, to buy and sell land and plots of land where facilities would be built and so on and so forth. I don't know -- that is, I know, but perhaps it wouldn't be all right for me to say. I cannot say personally. But this was obstructed. It couldn't simply work because the authorities, the government, was not fully formed, not all the offices were distributed. That is why it was done at the Serb expense, that is, that the commercial outlets or plots were all either let or sold to members of the Party for Democratic Action, that is, Muslims, not Serbs. Perhaps one cannot say that there were pressures, but there were major requests to buy land from Serbs around town or purchase of business outlets, and people were talking. That was a constant topic in the town. I know that more prominent, eminent people were trying to calm people down, "well, don't sell, take it easy." But you know how people react when there is constant pressure and so on and so forth. Well, perhaps I didn't list it all. You told me to be brief, but I hope it's all clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what were your plans? Let me first go back a minute. When you did the takeover in Prijedor on the 30th of April, you took over the institutions within the town of Prijedor. And there was no attempt to go into those areas that were dominated by other ethnic groups, particularly the Kozarac area and the Brdo area, Stari Grad. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stari Grad isn't an integral part of the town. There was no problem there so I don't know how to tell you. It's practically in the centre of the town, except that a long time ago, that is where Prijedor started to grow, so there was no problem about that. And over here, I mean at Hambarine, and that other side, people went normally until those checkpoints grew up there, which didn't allow people to get through. I hope that I've answered that, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took over authority in the town, did you set up checkpoints in the town of Prijedor? Did the Serb police, and whatever other forces were assisting them, set up checkpoints, set up things like machine-guns in front of the Municipal Assembly, guard posts, checkpoints leading into the town, for example at Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean it's next to the bridge. You cross the Sana, and that's where Tukovi is. There were checkpoints. The checkpoints were mostly at the exits to the town, not all over the town because otherwise it would look like a state of war. But I don't remember that there was a machine-gun in front of the municipal hall. No, I think there was one, but it was only after the attack. That is, a few days later. They were afraid that another attack might ensue. But I don't remember whether there was something before the attack on the 30th or after that. I think it was after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you know about the checkpoints because part of your duties was to supply the checkpoints with food. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the elected authorities were removed in Prijedor, at that time, Muslims still remained in control of Kozarac and the Brdo region, Hambarine and the Brdo region. Correct? And they did, as you said, set up checkpoints to prevent armed individuals from going -- well, let's not talk about the purpose. They did set up checkpoints in Kozarac and Hambarine, the Muslims set up their own. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, set up checkpoints and armed men, well that could apply to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you had this plan to take over Prijedor, what was your plan about what you were going to do with the Muslims that were so concentrated in areas like Kozarac and Brdo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was being planned? Well, there was no such plan. I don't know why you're talking about this in this way. As far as I know, there was no such conversations. There were talks. It wasn't plans. People were talking, saying that the problems in the town and municipality have reached such proportions that something had to be done, that such a situation couldn't really go on, and during the half hour, that is how long the meeting lasted, I don't know whether there was even a theoretical chance to prepare such plans. But as far as I know, nobody ever adopted such plans. What happened what happened because there was an attack on the town, because people were killed at Hambarine, and because the army had responded to that attack there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, there was no plan to change the demographics of Prijedor, and the SDS, those of you involved in the takeover, had no problem with holding a fair election where the majority would be allowed to speak and perhaps another Muslim government would be elected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was this problem. If you managed to come by some information during the talks that I had in Puharska, in Stari Grad, with those people in Kozarac, with that Mr. Solo from Cela, it was always said as I said it, and I heard others say it, once I believe Mr. Stakic was present at such a meeting when Mr. Solo came with his covillagers, with the imam and people from the neighbourhood community office. And we asked them -- at all our meetings, we asked them to maintain law and order in all those localities and have the political matters settled later on. Let's organise new elections, if they want the government, then let them have it. But we're saying that while the situation was such as it is, it was simply guard localities and people and everybody, and I remember that is what these talks and conversations were about. Now, if need be, you can ask those people, too. Mr. Solo is in Prijedor. I saw him several times, and we greeted one another, and we're glad to see one another. And he thanked me. But it doesn't really matter how I helped. Mr. Rifat Kurtovic who was in Stari Grad and he is in Prijedor, too. He is now in his house. Muhedin Saric, he is the principal of the school in Kozarac right now, and he can also, I mean, confirm this. And my neighbours over there, I'm told they still live. Bego Celic's family, Mina Alijagic's family, they are there. And the Kapetanovic family, and the Ivica Vidikovic's family, they are there. They can confirm what were those conversations like, and they were pretty honest. Now, what somebody from other parties said -- and I won't call them nationalistic. They were national parties, the SDA and such. Now what they wanted, what their plans were, that is another matter. People sold lots of their property, and thus they got money to buy arms, for the Muslims and for the Croats. For Serbs, then, yes, because there was fear around. But we were always the last one, just as when the party was formed. That is not the party, but the movement. Everybody did it before us, and we still believed in Yugoslavia, and we believed that Yugoslavia would survive and that we would preserve it and that we would be its path. But you see, it failed, not the Yugoslavia has remained in part, and now also this one has fallen apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff issue a poster that was put around the town after the takeover explaining the reasons for the takeover and that in the future, there would be elections after peace was established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this was discussed. Some elders, those not -- those who had more experience said that perhaps it would be a wise thing to do. But I do not know where and in how many places those posters were. Quite possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about the negotiations that you took part in. Is it correct that then you were negotiating for the disarmament of those people in places like Brdo, Kozarac, and Cela, to have them turn their weapons in to the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not within that context. It was discussed to disarm some paramilitary forms, and those who were in the field, that they should control the situation because there were also parts of the police force, and that those who for all sorts of their personal reasons had somehow procured personal weapons should not be allowed to do anything on their own, to avoid any misfortune because, you know, if somebody resorts to arms -- well, you know the situation was tense anyway, so that all sorts of stupid things could have happened. And as you heard, yes, it did happen. Aliskovic, and I don't know whether somebody ordered him to do it or not, that is also possible, but he did it. And then those in Kozarac, and then, well, you see that's how it started. The Serbs, they didn't kill anyone, nor did they start anything. They didn't attack anyone in their convoys, in their patrols or anything, or at their checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about the negotiations. You mentioned Mr. Solo. Is that someone from Cela? I'm sorry, do you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. But he's an imam. He's a hodza. That's what he was in Cela. That's what I know. A man, a nice man, and he worked for the humanitarian organisation Merhamet in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also negotiated with several other people of Muslim ethnicity or non-Serb ethnicity. Dr. Esad Sadikovic was one of them. Can you tell us who he is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right, I don't mind. Those were not negotiations. Those were talks, they weren't negotiations. But never mind. He's a well-known doctor in Prijedor, a physician, whose children attended the school of which I was the principal. That man respected me, and I knew that he was a nice gentleman, and I think he was a member of the reformist forces or something of that sort. At his initiative, the meeting took place, and I asked that this meeting be organised, and the two of us went up to Brdo near Carakovo and talked there with people. The imam was there, and the SDA president, and the president of the neighbourhood community there, and some other people, I don't remember. And we had agreed that they would look after that area, and they would keep an eye on those young people who have hot blood to prevent them from doing something silly. And there was the Territorial Defence who also had their arms pursuant to a decision of the Council for people's defence of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say the president of the SDA, do you mean for Prijedor or for Kozarac? Are you referring to Mr. Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not talking about any of them. I mean the president of that part of the SDA which had to do with that neighbourhood community. It is a branch of the SDA, whoever it was, when I spoke about Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
