utterances.text: Sir, did you speak to Becir Medunjanin in your talks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once. There was a meeting. It was the president of the SDS party, Mr. Miskovic, and senator, Mr. Srdja insisted on that. And a man from Kozarac came, Mr. Medunjanin was one of them, and there was an MP, a young one, what's his name? Sejmenovic. And a fair-haired engineer, I forget what he did in the municipality, but he taught physics. Before that, he was also my pupil. I can't remember what his name was because it was a long time ago. They were young people, and we discussed the situation with them in Kozarac and at the checkpoint and with the weapons carried by those who were outside the Territorial Defence. And as far as I can remember, in that part which belonged to the Territorial Defence of Kozarac, in Kozarusa, that is, it has already been transformed into a large barracks with many armed men who were under the guise of Territorial Defence. But that Territorial Defence wasn't all that numerous. However, there was a large number of people who were armed there. But, right. The chief reason was the behaviour at the checkpoint and the request that the policemen who, in the organisational sense of the word, were under the public security station in Prijedor should perform their work within that public security centre, that is, to look after the peace and order, to enforce law, and to be loyal adherents of that power. Well, there was a problem of the patches they would have. When they said that they would never manage to prevail upon those policemen, to put the patches of the said police, because the distribution of colours was different on the flags, then we agreed that it should be so. But we said that those who would arm themselves paramilitarily outside the Territorial Defence, we asked them to take the weapons from them and to keep them in the Territorial Defence and that they should enforce the order in Kozarac, in that neighbourhood community. And they promised to talk, but as we could see, that talk bore no fruit because the military, the army column was attacked. People were killed, and then the army's ultimatum ensued. And so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the interests of time and an orderly examination, please limit your answer to the question. The question I asked, much of what you just said you've told us before. The question I asked was did you speak to Mr. Medunjanin. And you began your answer with yes. Now I want to ask you, sir, is it correct that you knew Mr. Medunjanin as a colleague from the schools? He was a teacher like you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him. I'd only heard about him. I think he was chief of the police at that time. Otherwise, yes, he was a teacher. I've heard about that. But I didn't know him, and I didn't talk with him directly. We all talked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Dedo Crnalic, you knew him. He was a well-known figure, owned a restaurant in Prijedor. And he participated in those talks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, these talks in Stari Grad were, up to a point, the result of the initiative Dr. Sadikovic or Dr. Crnalic, the two of them went with me to Stari Grad. There was a large number of people there. And now I've forgotten who else was there. I think that Miskovic was there, but I'm not quite sure. I don't know. I know that I wasn't alone. And the folk there know me well, the Muslims who had grown up with me because that is practically the centre of the town and they trusted me. And Mr. Dedo, he had known me all my life. He knew what kind of a person I was, so that they trusted us. They received us there, and we talked. And then whatever the case, I think another one turned up, I think his name was Hadzja, and another man called Beganovic who had taken weapons from the depot of the Territorial Defence, which was there and fired and threatened some girls, but as far as I know, nobody got killed. And they were also seized by fear and they did not say anything about the government even though they disagreed with them and the promise, because there were a large number of people, 2 or 300 people who were present at those talks, many of my acquaintances and pupils, and we agreed that they would do their utmost to prevent any excesses, and that was the end of those talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, when the Muslim representatives refused to put on the patch of the Serbian Republic -- the police refused to put on the patch of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they refused to turn in their weapons, who did you report that to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I simply participated, I said. Perhaps I've said it already two or three times. Perhaps it is funny to talk in this way about it. It is immodest. I participated because I was invited. Otherwise it wasn't my duty to do it. It was up to the public security station, that is, Mr. Simo Drljaca who was the head of the centre. The weapons -- the police wasn't asked to hand over the weapons. What we asked was he asked from the official police in Kozarac was to take the weapons from those who represented some kind of paramilitary formations and were firing shots around Kozarac. There are even photographs of them doing that. And they refused to do it. And under the pretext that they were not wearing that sign, at least that is what I understood them to say. Now, who it was -- who is it that the chief of the police sent his report to, I don't know. I guess it was to his superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you speak in the Crisis Staff about these talks or in the National Defence Council, did you speak - and I don't mean you personally, but in the group - was there discussion about these talks with the Muslims from Kozarac and Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably we did. I don't remember exactly. There must have been a discussion. It was impossible for these things to be happening without anybody talking about them. It seems to me that people were glad there were such discussions and such talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of a Howitzer battery and anti-aircraft weapons being moved to Prijedor in early May following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can assume, if you want me to guess and if you want to hear my guesses, I can share them with you. The Howitzers and the anti-aircraft guns, they're all weapons belonging to the army. And if the corps command issued an order for part of the army to return to Prijedor, to the barracks, from wherever they had been, it is possible that the Howitzers and other artillery pieces arrived on the order of the region command or Colonel Arsic, that is, or anybody else that was authorised by him to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that we have the context, at that time, part of the 343rd Brigade was deployed along the front in Croatia where there was a cease-fire, but no peace. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. It certainly was not peace. It was a cease-fire. Peace arrived only later. I suppose you're right. It must have been a cease-fire, and I know that one part of the brigade was up there. Or maybe even the whole brigade. I'm just tying this question to your earlier question. Probably one part of the brigade was up there, and the other part of the brigade was ordered to return back to the barracks in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you present at any discussions that would give you an insight into why these heavy weapons were moved into the Prijedor Municipality after the takeover and who they were anticipated to be used against?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attend such talks. Can you imagine such weapons arriving and talks involving such weapons? It was the garrison command that had all the authority, and the orders are just not discussed. If the corps commander issued an order, then the troops were there to carry out those orders, not to ask any questions, either them or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Sir, you're aware that among the people that you had these talks with, Esad Sadikovic, Dedo Crnalic, Becir Medunjanin, that they are all were killed -- were all sent to the Omarska camp and killed. You're aware of that, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been officially informed about that. But I heard it on the grapevine. I heard it from other people, that they had been incarcerated in Omarska. Now as to whether they were killed there or not, I don't know. I know that they are not in Prijedor. I also haven't heard stories about them being anywhere else. What has happened to them, I don't know. Whether they were still alive, whether they joined with their families or not, I don't know. And I can't give you any official answer to this question. They're just -- they're rumours and what people are guessing. So I can't give either a yes or a no answer to this question of yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct that among members of the SDS in Prijedor, and other persons sympathetic to that party, one of the most infamous figures in the history of Prijedor would have been Slavko Ecimovic who led the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have used a strong -- very, very powerful attribute. This Slavko Ecimovic was one of my students. He was his maths and physics teacher. He was a wonderful guy. He spent a lot of time working in Zagreb as a taxi driver. I did not see him nor was I anywhere close to him when these operation were taking place. I was surprised to hear that he was the leader of those 125 or 150 men who were involved in the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it was also well-known that when this attack by 120 or men with rifles, that you were quoted in one of the articles earlier saying did not have a ghost of a chance, that Slavko Ecimovic was arrested, he was captured during that operation when it was defeated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did comment upon that. And I said that there was not a slight chance because there were checkpoints. There was the army along the Sana River, next to the bridge. I know that a number of people were killed at that checkpoint. I don't know how many of them, towards Gomjenica, they entered through the private houses, across the Stari Grad some people were killed there because there was army there as well, and they had headed towards the city centre. But the news travelled very fast, and the army regrouped its ranks. People got very soon connected by telephones, and the army neutralised that attack, although they managed to arrive as far as the Municipal Assembly. I believe that 16 of them were killed, and a number of them were wounded. However, that attack was brought to an end. It was interrupted. As for Slavko and for his lot, I don't know. I suppose that he was captured, maybe taken to prison for interrogation. Because he was the one who carried out this attack, this armed attack. I already said that. Maybe the comparison is not very nice, but when the Serbs were taking over, no lives were lost, no shot was fired. But when this attack was carried out, it ended differently. But that's another story. It would have been best if nothing had happened. If there were negotiations and agreements at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was then called the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if Mr. Alija Izetbegovic had -- I apologise. I thought maybe I should say this, because it seems very important to me, but you don't want me to say it, I apologise. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd request you to just answer the question. We really don't want to discuss right now the politics of the entire war. We're talking about Mr. Ecimovic who you described as a wonderful man, and who other witnesses or at least one witness has described as a man of integrity who led the attempts to retake Prijedor after the elected government was overthrown was captured. Sir, such a high-profile figure, wouldn't it be well-known what happened to him, his fate? Didn't you know, he, as one of your former students, weren't you aware that he went to the Omarska camp and was killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was arrested and taken away. Whether he was killed or not, I don't know. Maybe the way you worded it was a bit different. He was a young person, and he was handsome. He was resourceful. His life was well organised. He worked in Zagreb. He started helping his family. I don't know whether he was married or not. He had been my student, and I knew him rather well. So I was really taken by surprise when I heard that he was the leader of that attack. I did hear stories about him being taken to Omarska and about his unfortunate lot. I myself was never in Omarska or in Keraterm. I can't say I'm glad that I wasn't there, but if what happened, what is alleged to have happened really, really happened, then it is a disgrace for all of us, for my people, for all of us, for my people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn now to the Trnopolje camp for a moment. You told us that this was a centre set up to help those who didn't have a home or who came there voluntarily. You said that buses and convoys came there, trains, carrying people outside of Prijedor. How many thousands of individuals do you think passed through the Trnopolje centre in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe 6 or 7.000 people altogether. If some of them left by trains or by buses, I believe their total number was 2 or 3.000. Some of them returned to Prijedor, to their homes. Some left with the UNHCR. About 1.450 men altogether were taken by buses to Karlovac. And between 200 and 300 who remained and left on my insisting. So altogether, I believe that the grand total was between 6 and 7.000. I don't know exactly. Maybe you could use the information that the Red Cross could provide you with. They had the list of those they issued with certificates, and they are the ones who could maybe tell you how many certificates they issued to people who asked for those certificates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we just have a minutes left today. Using your testimony, as I understand your testimony, this centre was dealing with a humanitarian crisis, that there were thousands of people, they didn't have beds. You acknowledged that some of them had to dig outside toilets, that there was a problem they had to be fed. This was, would you agree, a huge humanitarian crisis involving thousands of people from the municipality of Prijedor. Correct? And these were not suspects; these were innocent people according to your testimony who were there for humanitarian reasons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply put, because of the war operations in Hambarine, in Kozarac, they fled that area to avoid getting killed. They were not incarcerated. They were not expunged. I don't know whether you understand the military terminology. There was a mop-up operation against those who had attacked the military convoy in order to disarm them. And there was shooting going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you how they got there. My question was, there was, according to your testimony, a huge humanitarian crisis. For that reason, you say, the centre was set up and that you were dealing with feeding, trying to provide housing, or at least a place to sleep on the ground or on the floor, for thousands of people who were citizens of Prijedor who were not prisoners or suspected of crime. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They fled because of war operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can just answer the following questions briefly: What is the distance from the Trnopolje camp to the Municipal Assembly building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some 10 kilometres, maybe more. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the approximate distance from the Trnopolje camp to Maricka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You promised you wouldn't use the word "camp." About the same distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that Milomir Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, did you ever see him visit the Trnopolje centre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember of such a thing happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why the president of the municipality did not go to the centre where thousands of people from his municipality were homeless, living under, according to your testimony, very, very bleak conditions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe you should ask him. Maybe you should have asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes your testimony of today. May I ask you, what was true also for the last days, please don't contact any of the parties and please don't discuss the issues of your testimony together with anybody, also not with any representative of your embassy or consulate or any other person that may be at the same time being here in The Hague for the purpose of testimony in this or in another case. We'll restart on Monday, in principle, in Courtroom II, save Courtroom I would be -- until now it's not foreseeable, Courtroom I would be available. So may I ask now the usher escort --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: , Your Honour, could I make a special request. We have a copy of the article I'd like him to review. There's also another fairly lengthy document I'd like him to have so he could be prepared for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, if we could have a copy of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be only fair. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As indicated some days, or -- some days before or even last week, the Trial Chamber has compiled a guidance on issues to be addressed in final briefs and/or closing arguments. And for a better understanding of this, there's no doubt at all that as regards factual issues, the burden of proof is with the Prosecution, and it's not necessarily that the Defence give some comments on factual issues. Nevertheless, it's the right if the Defence so want, also to address factual issues mentioned here, especially addressed to the Office of the Prosecution. However, the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that these guidelines not only serve as a judicial hint, but also serve as the best possible way to grant the right to be heard to the parties on issues, especially legal issues, that not yet have been resolved by this Tribunal. So therefore, please regard this in part as a request, in part as an invitation. And for the transcript, no doubt the absence of a question in relation to certain facts does not mean that those facts have already been established beyond a reasonable doubt. These are only special facts where the Trial Chamber, for this period of time, has concrete questions, especially in the direction of the OTP. May I ask the usher, please, to distribute three copies to the Prosecution, three copies to the Defence. And then please, one as an attachment for today's transcript. Thank you. Let us mark the document just right now distributed by the Prosecution with the next available exhibit number for the Prosecution. That would be S, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: S431, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S431, provisionally marked under this number. Any other issues to be raised before the weekend? This is not the case. This concludes not only today's hearing, but also this week's hearing. It was a long, hard week. And I have to thank all the participants assisting us, and I wish a good weekend to everybody. The trial stays adjourned until Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
